books.title: Three Men in a Boat
books.author: Jerome K. Jerome
books.desc: Three friends who believe they are suffering from overwork take a boating holiday up the Thames, with a fox terrier named Montmorency.
about: J., the narrator, and his friends George and Harris decide that they are suffering from "overwork" and need a rest. After rejecting a country stay and a sea trip, they settle on a boating holiday up the River Thames, from Kingston upon Thames to Oxford, camping on the way, accompanied by J.'s dog Montmorency. Packing, cooking, pitching the tent, towing the boat and dealing with other river users all lead to comic disasters, interrupted by anecdotes and reflections on the places they pass.

Jerome's comic travelogue mixes slapstick, gentle irony and occasional lyrical or historical passages. Its humour comes largely from the narrator's self-mocking voice and from the small frustrations of everyday life.

Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog) was published in 1889. George and Harris were based on Jerome's real friends George Wingrave and Carl Hentschel; the dog Montmorency, according to Jerome, was entirely fictional.
books.author_short: English writer and humorist (1859–1927), best known for the comic travelogue Three Men in a Boat.
author_long: Jerome Klapka Jerome was born in Walsall, in the English Midlands, on 2 May 1859. When his father died in 1871, he left school at thirteen to work as a clerk for the London and North Western Railway, and later tried various occupations, including three years as an actor. He died on 14 June 1927.
His works include the essay collection Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow (1886), Three Men in a Boat (1889) and its sequel Three Men on the Bummel.

books.title: The Man Who Was Thursday
books.author: G. K. Chesterton
books.desc: A poet turned police detective infiltrates a council of anarchists, each named after a day of the week, and finds that nothing is what it seems.
about: In the London suburb of Saffron Park, the poet Gabriel Syme argues with Lucian Gregory, an anarchist poet, about whether poetry is rebellion or order. Syme is in fact a member of a secret police corps devoted to fighting anarchism. Gregory takes him to an underground meeting place, and Syme manages to have himself elected to the post of "Thursday" on the central anarchist council, whose seven members are named after the days of the week and are led by the enormous and terrifying Sunday.

Subtitled "A Nightmare", Chesterton's novel begins as a comic spy thriller and becomes a metaphysical fable about order and chaos, doubt and faith. It is prefaced by a poem addressed to his friend Edmund Clerihew Bentley.
The Man Who Was Thursday was published in 1908.
books.author_short: English writer, critic and Christian apologist (1874–1936), creator of the priest-detective Father Brown.
author_long: Gilbert Keith Chesterton was born in Kensington, London, on 29 May 1874. A prolific journalist, essayist, poet and novelist, he was received into the Catholic Church in 1922. He died on 14 June 1936.
He created the priest-detective Father Brown and wrote works of Christian apologetics such as Orthodoxy and The Everlasting Man. His novels include The Man Who Was Thursday (1908).

books.title: Sons and Lovers
books.author: D. H. Lawrence
books.desc: In a Nottinghamshire mining town, a young man grows up torn between his devotion to his mother and his love for two very different women.
about: Gertrude Coppard, a refined young woman, marries Walter Morel, a rough and lively miner, after meeting him at a Christmas dance, but the marriage soon turns bitter in the poverty of the mining village of Bestwood. Gertrude pours her affection into her sons, first William, then Paul. As Paul grows up and begins to paint, he falls into a relationship with Miriam, a farmer's daughter, and later with Clara Dawes, a woman separated from her husband Baxter, while his mother's hold over him remains strong.

Lawrence's novel explores family conflict, class, work in the mines and the emotional and sexual development of a young man, with a powerful sense of the landscape and community of the Nottinghamshire coalfield.
Sons and Lovers was published in 1913 by Duckworth in London and Mitchell Kennerley in New York. Before publication it was usually called Paul Morel.
books.author_short: English novelist, poet and essayist (1885–1930), author of Sons and Lovers, Women in Love and Lady Chatterley's Lover.
author_long: David Herbert Lawrence was born on 11 September 1885 in Eastwood, Nottinghamshire, the fourth child of a miner and a former pupil-teacher. He won a scholarship to Nottingham High School and worked as a pupil-teacher before turning to writing. He died on 2 March 1930.

His novels Sons and Lovers (1913), The Rainbow (1915), Women in Love (1920) and Lady Chatterley's Lover (1928) were the subject of censorship trials because of their frank treatment of sexuality. He also wrote poetry, short stories, plays, travel books and criticism.

books.title: The Velveteen Rabbit
books.author: Margery Williams
books.desc: A stuffed toy rabbit longs to become Real, and learns from the old Skin Horse that only a child's love can make it happen.
about: A velveteen rabbit is given to a little boy as a Christmas present and soon forgotten among the grander mechanical toys of the nursery. The wise old Skin Horse tells him that toys become Real when a child loves them for a long, long time. Gradually the Rabbit becomes the Boy's favourite companion, shabby from being loved, until the Boy falls ill.
This short story for children speaks with simplicity and tenderness about love, growing old, loss and what it means to be real.
The Velveteen Rabbit, or How Toys Become Real first appeared in Harper's Bazaar in 1921 and was published as a book in 1922, with illustrations by William Nicholson.
books.author_short: English-American author of children's books (1881–1944), best known for The Velveteen Rabbit.
author_long: Margery Winifred Williams was born in London in 1881. She published her first novel, for adults, in 1902. After her marriage to Francesco Bianco she wrote as Margery Williams Bianco, and from 1921 lived with her family in Greenwich Village, New York. She died on 4 September 1944.
The Velveteen Rabbit (1922) was her first American work and remains her most famous. She received a Newbery Honor for Winterbound.

books.title: Captain Blood
books.author: Rafael Sabatini
books.desc: An Irish doctor unjustly condemned for treating a wounded rebel is sold as a slave in Barbados and escapes to become a famous buccaneer.
about: In 1685 Peter Blood, an Irish physician who has once been a soldier and sailor, lives quietly in Bridgwater, Somerset, tending his geraniums. Called to treat a rebel wounded at the battle of Sedgemoor during the Monmouth Rebellion, he is arrested and condemned for treason by Judge Jeffreys at the Bloody Assizes. Transported to Barbados and sold to the brutal Colonel Bishop, he wins the friendship of Bishop's niece Arabella, then escapes with other convicts, among them the young navigator Jeremy Pitt, and becomes a buccaneer captain in the Caribbean, rival of the cruel Levasseur.

Sabatini's swashbuckling novel combines sea battles, honour and romance with real historical events. Its picture of the Caribbean plantations and of enslaved Africans reflects the language and attitudes of its time.

The adventures of Captain Blood first appeared as short stories in Premier Magazine in 1920 and 1921, which Sabatini wove into a continuous novel, Captain Blood: His Odyssey, published in 1922. The first part was inspired by the real story of Henry Pitman, a surgeon transported to Barbados after the Monmouth Rebellion.
books.author_short: Italian-born British writer of historical adventure novels (1875–1950), author of Scaramouche and Captain Blood.
author_long: Rafael Sabatini was born on 29 April 1875 in Jesi, Italy, to an English mother and an Italian father. He worked for about a quarter of a century before achieving success with Scaramouche in 1921. He died in Switzerland on 13 February 1950.

His best-known novels are The Sea Hawk (1915), Scaramouche (1921) and Captain Blood (1922). His headstone bears the first line of Scaramouche: "He was born with a gift of laughter and a sense that the world was mad."
